title: TypeScript Generics Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on TypeScript generics: generic functions, interfaces and classes, extends constraints, default type parameters, keyof and indexed access types. Ordered from the mental model through workflow, usage and mistakes to a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Generics Mental Model
points: Definition: a generic is a type-level parameter, `function id<T>(x: T): T`, so one declaration works for many types without losing type info
Generic vs any: `any` discards the type; `T` links input to output, so `id(5)` returns the literal type `5`, not `any`
Type parameters are erased at runtime; they exist only for the compiler, so you cannot do `new T()` or `typeof T`
Type arguments are usually inferred from call arguments: `id('a')` infers the literal `T = 'a'`; pass explicitly with `id<string>('a')` when inference fails
Interview Point: What problem do generics solve over `any`? Are generics available at runtime? When does TypeScript infer T versus needing it explicitly?

chapters.title: Generic Functions, Interfaces and Classes
points: Generic function: `function first<T>(a: T[]): T | undefined { return a[0]; }`; arrow form in .tsx needs `<T,>(x: T) => x`
Generic interface: `interface Box<T> { value: T }` then `Box<number>`; also generic call signatures `interface Fn<T> { (x: T): T }`
Generic class: `class Stack<T> { private items: T[] = []; push(x: T) { this.items.push(x) } pop(): T | undefined { return this.items.pop() } }`; `new Stack<number>()`
Generic type alias: `type Pair<A, B> = [A, B]`; multiple params are comma-separated and each must be supplied unless defaulted
Static members cannot reference the class type parameter, because T belongs to the instance side only
Interview Point: How do you declare a generic class and instantiate it? Why can't a static member use T? Interface vs type alias for generics?

chapters.title: Constraints with extends
points: Constraint syntax: `function len<T extends { length: number }>(x: T) { return x.length }` accepts string, array, or any object with length
Without a constraint, T is unknown-like and property access errors: `x.length` fails on a bare `T`
The constraint limits what callers may pass but T keeps the specific type: `len([1, 2])` still has `T = number[]`, not the constraint type (`len('abc')` infers `T = string`)
Constraining one param by another: `function pick<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]`
Constructor constraint: `T extends new (...a: any[]) => object` lets you accept classes and `new` them
Interview Point: What does `extends` mean in a generic constraint versus class inheritance? Why does a bare T not allow `.length`? How do you make one type parameter depend on another?

chapters.title: Defaults, keyof and Indexed Access
points: Default type parameter: `interface Res<T = unknown> { data: T }` so `Res` alone means `Res<unknown>`; defaulted params must come after required ones
A default is used when T cannot be inferred and is not given; it must also satisfy any constraint: `<T extends object = {}>`
`keyof T` yields the union of T's property names: `keyof {a: 1; b: 2}` is `'a' | 'b'`; `keyof any[]` includes `number` and method names
Indexed access type: `T[K]` is the type of property K, e.g. `User['id']`; `T[number]` gives array element type; `T[keyof T]` gives union of all value types
Typed getter combining all three: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K] { return o[k] }`, so wrong keys fail at compile time and the return type is exact
Interview Point: What does `keyof` return, and for arrays or index signatures? How does `T[K]` keep the return type precise? When is a default type parameter applied?

chapters.title: Common Generic Mistakes
points: Using `T` only once in a signature (`function f<T>(x: T): void`) adds nothing; each type parameter should relate at least two positions
Casting `as T` or returning `{} as T` hides errors; the compiler cannot verify a value really is T
Over-constraining with `T extends string` then returning a literal fails: `return 'a'` is not assignable to `T`, since T could be a narrower literal
Narrowing a generic value with `typeof x === 'string'` does not narrow `T` itself; use overloads or conditional types
Forgetting `K extends keyof T` and typing the key as `string` loses safety and errors with implicit any on `o[k]`
Interview Point: Why is a type parameter used only once a smell? Why can't you return a concrete value for T? How do you debug a failed inference?

chapters.title: Generics Cheat Sheet
points: Function: `function f<T>(x: T): T`; Interface: `interface I<T> { v: T }`; Class: `class C<T> {}`; Alias: `type A<T> = T[]`
Constrain: `<T extends U>`; depend: `<K extends keyof T>`; default: `<T = string>` (defaults last)
`keyof T` = key union; `T[K]` = value type; `T[number]` = array element; `T[keyof T]` = all values
Pattern: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]` is the idiom for type-safe property access
Rules: erased at runtime, inferred from args, no statics with T, avoid `as T`, use T at least twice
Interview Point: Write a type-safe `pick` from memory. Which constraint ties a key to an object? What is the order rule for defaults?
